linguisticReconstructions.claim: The jamu is a patrilineal clan name: it designates membership in a descent group, not an individual filiation to the father.

The origin narrative of the Bambara dynasties has the two brothers Baramangolo and Niangolo cross the river without a canoe; from this crossing the family name Kulibali (Kurubari) is drawn, from kulu "canoe" and the privative bali. The source that states it immediately adds that other versions exist.

casteOrSocialFunction.value: The dictionary of jamuw gives the entry Kùlibàli the status hɔ́rɔn, then tontigi among the Bamana, the Maninka and the Minianka, then numu (blacksmith) in Wassoulou. The jamu thus carries both a free condition and, depending on the area, a hereditary craft function.

sources.title: EthniAfrica — fiche du peuple Bambara, organisation clanique
sources.notes: Taken from the "Clan organisation" chapter of the Bambara people's fiche.

sources.title: Beyond the Mali Empire — A New Paradigm for the Sunjata Epic
sources.notes: Jansen, Jan, Universiteit Leiden. Critical work on the transmission of the epic and on the jamu as a social institution rather than as historical memory; used here for the nature of the jamu, not to date an ancestor.

sources.title: General History of Africa, V: Africa from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century
sources.notes: UNESCO, General History of Africa, vol. V, ed. B. A. Ogot, 1992; consulted in full text. Chapter 12, "From the Niger to the Volta" (M. Izard and J. Ki-Zerbo): the sanankunya between the Kulibali (Kurubari) and the Keita or the Ture, given as an indication of long-standing relations between Bambara and Malinke (p. 330); the etymology kulu "canoe" + privative bali, drawn from the crossing of the river without a canoe, accompanied by the source's own note that other versions exist (p. 330 n. 7); the genealogy of Mamari Kulibali, known as Biton (1712-1755), great-grandson of Baramangolo through Kaladian, Danfassari and Soma (p. 330-333). Chapter 13, "The states and cultures of the Upper Guinean coast" (C. Wondji): the migration of the Kongo-Vai from the upper Niger under the leadership of the Camara clan, towards Bopolou and then the Mano and Moa rivers, and the correlated displacement of the Kono and the Vai towards the coasts of Liberia and Sierra Leone (p. 375-377).

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Onomastic annex of the Bamadaba, an electronic Bambara-French dictionary supplementing the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA); the clan names annex is identified as such by Vydrin, "Vers une lexicographie mandingue sur la base de grands corpus annotés", Mandenkan 63, 2020, p. 89-110. 375 entries in MDF format, consulted in the complete file. The file provides no legend for its markers, and the reading adopted is the one the file imposes: \ca carries the Mandingo status terms themselves (nùmu, jèli, hɔ́rɔn, garanke, finɛ, tontigi, wage, gesere); \sn is read as senankun because the Kúyate entry annotates its own line "\sn Keyita" with a caveat stating that this particular relation is a friendly agreement and not a senankuya. The \sn links are not systematically reciprocal from one entry to another: each pair is therefore cited according to the entry that carries it, named in the claim or the gap.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, number 38, 2002, p. 175-197. Field survey in Mali. She states what the pact obliges: the relation holds in perpetuity for all descendants of the two lineages, marriage between them is prohibited — variably applied today, she specifies — and mutual assistance is owed without reservation. Cited for the obligation itself; it does not name the pair in this fiche, which is carried by the entries cited alongside it.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, number 184, 2006, p. 687 and following. Cited for the caution it carries: the idea that joking kinship would ease conflicts is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict-resolution studies, thus as a discourse to be analysed rather than as a measured effect. The starting page is verified, the ending page is not.

gaps.reason: Coulibaly transcribes the Manding Kulibali, which the dictionary of jamuw also writes as Kùlubàli and which the General History of Africa gives in the form Kurubari. None of these spellings corresponds to a distinct line of origin in the sources consulted.
